1:
The chapter opens without a subject — and he said unto Moses — and two of them notice the disorder and solve it in opposite ways. Ellicott takes it as a seam: the missing nominative is best explained by the insertion here of the Book of the Covenant, originally a distinct document, so that this verse once followed directly on Moses drew near unto the thick darkness where God was. Clarke reports instead the complaint of Calmet, who finds the same want of order and repairs it by rearranging the events: God laid all the laws before Moses on the mount and told him that once the people had ratified them they were to come up again with the elders. Gill asks the question and leaves it: who said? no doubt a divine Person. Ellicott adds that these seventy are not the judges appointed in the eighteenth chapter, who did not yet exist, but the heads of tribes and families who had held authority in Egypt.

That last point is where Calvin sees a difficulty, since the seventy are elsewhere not chosen until the people have left Sinai, yet appear here before the Law is promulgated. His solution is that each tribe had appointed six governors of its own before they came to the mount, making up the number, and that when Moses asked to be relieved the government was transferred to men already honourably distinguished. He also explains why the ascent was needed: the Tables had to be fetched before the tabernacle was consecrated, since an ark with nothing in it would leave the sanctuary empty.

The two verses prescribe a graded approach, and Calvin counts the steps: a station for the people, worshipping afar off; the elders and priests admitted closer, as witnesses of what they would see; and Moses alone received into the higher glory. He insists the verbs are imperative and not past, since what is reported is not yet what was done but what God commanded. Clarke gives the same arrangement as topography — the people at the foot, Aaron with his sons and the elders perhaps half way up, Moses alone to the summit — and notes that the people had heard the voice less distinctly, like the grumbling of distant thunder.

Henry and Wesley draw the devotional lesson, Wesley's two notes here being abridgements of Henry's at the same verses. Before they came near they must worship: so we must enter God's gates with humble and solemn adorations, as those who know their distance. Henry presses it with a question Wesley drops: are great princes approached with the profound reverences of the body, and shall not the soul that draws near to God be bowed before him? Both make Moses a type of Christ, who as high priest entered alone into the most holy place; and Henry adds that when a communion is begun between God and us it shall never fail on his side, if it do not first fail on ours.

One question of substance remains, and it divides them. Henry says Moses laid before them all the precepts of the foregoing chapters, and did not lead them blindfold into the covenant nor teach a devotion that was the daughter of ignorance; and he turns their unanimous consent into a lament, that people will not always stay in the good mind they sometimes seem to be in. Keil restricts the phrase much more narrowly. All the words of Jehovah cannot mean the decalogue, since the people had heard that directly from God; it means the words about altars that follow it, while all the rights means the chapters of judgments — and the recital with the people's answer was not the covenant but the preparation for it, since they had to know what was imposed and to declare themselves willing before it could be made.
3:
What Moses recited is still contested. Clarke includes the decalogue outright, with the laws and ordinances of the four preceding chapters. Gill excludes it, since the people had heard the ten from the Lord themselves, and confines the recital to the judicial laws of the two chapters before; he also sets aside the rabbinic list of Noachide commands, sabbath, honouring parents and the red heifer, as either already known or not yet given. Ellicott takes a middle course: Moses gave an outline, the general purport and main heads but not the details, since otherwise there would have been no need to read the book to them afterwards. His note on their answer is the sharpest thing here — they gave their adhesion willingly, feeling the laws to be holy, just and good, not yet knowing how hard perfect obedience would prove.

Over the writing itself two of them collide. Ellicott observes that the mediator's familiarity with writing is presumed throughout the Pentateuch, one learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians being unlikely to lack so ordinary an Egyptian accomplishment. Wesley says the opposite: God probably taught him letters there on the mount, and he taught them to Israel, from whom they afterwards travelled to Greece and the other nations. Wesley adds that as soon as God separated a peculiar people he governed them by a written word, as he has ever since.

The altar and the twelve pillars are agreed in substance, divided in meaning. Clarke has the altar probably of turf, as had been commanded, with twelve unhewn stones round it, and reads the arrangement as a contract: the altar represents the throne of God and the stones the tribes, these being the two parties entering into covenant. Ellicott says the same, adding that the pillars were probably long stones set on end. Wesley has them set over against the altar with Moses passing to and fro between, and guesses each tribe knew its own pillar. Calvin gives the stones a quite different office. They stood by the altar according to the number of the tribes so the people might know they were not kept at a distance in token of rejection, but only that, conscious of their unworthiness, they might humble themselves: though removed far off they were still remembered before God, who embraced them all by these monuments, which bore no human shape, being heaps of stones and not images.

Who the young men were is settled twice, from different directions. Gill reports the rabbinic view that they were the firstborn, who served as priests before the priesthood was given to Aaron, and declines it: the objections are not easily refuted, and probably they were choice young men separated for the service without regard to birthright. Keil rejects that theory and one more — they were neither firstborn officiating by primogeniture nor, as Augustine held, sons of Aaron, but servants of Moses, the sprinkling being performed by him as mediator. Ellicott supplies the principle: even after the Levitical priesthood was instituted, any Israelite might slaughter the victim and lay the flesh on the altar, only the sprinkling and the kindling being reserved to the priest — here, before that priesthood existed, the sprinkling alone. The young men were used because their strength fitted them to deal with the animals, which is Clarke's account too and one of Calvin's two options.

Ellicott distinguishes the offerings: burnt offerings at once expiatory and signs of self-dedication, peace offerings expressions of gratitude, the two together marking thankfulness at being taken into covenant. Calvin sets the act in a wider frame, that covenants have in every age and among the heathen been accompanied with sacrifice, and makes the division of the blood — half on the altar, half kept in basins for the people — the symbol by which this covenant was ratified.
6:
Halving the blood is unusual and Ellicott says why: the sprinkling on the altar was the most essential part of every sacrifice, the act by which the victim, as representative of the offerer, was delivered up to God, and ordinarily all the blood was so devoted, only here being some needed for another purpose. Keil adds a philological distinction the others pass over: the half thrown on the altar was swung from the vessel, a different verb from the sprinkling done afterwards, and several young oxen had yielded blood enough for many to be caught by it.

What the division meant is agreed; where the custom came from is not agreed. Keil says the two halves had reference to the two parties, to be brought by the covenant into a living unity — then denies flatly that the rite had any connection whatever with the heathen customs adduced for comparison. Ellicott adduces them anyway: blood-communion rites were common throughout the East in connection with covenants, and he cites Homer, Herodotus, Xenophon and Tacitus for it, holding that such usages were felt to add force and sacredness. Clarke reaches the same mutuality without the comparative material: no covenant was reckoned binding until a sacrifice had been offered, and the two sprinklings showed both sides bound — God to support, defend and save, the people to fear, love and serve him.

The book itself is narrowly identified. Ellicott makes it the collection written overnight, running from the altar-law after the decalogue to the end of the promises, and observes that the people, having now heard the ipsissima verba spoken to Moses, repeated their earlier acceptance and added a general promise of obedience. Gill draws attention to what is easily missed, that the book was not only law: it contained God's promises to send his angel, drive out the Canaanites and put them in possession, so that there were promises on both sides — a restipulation of parties, which made it a formal covenant.

On whom the blood fell is disputed, and the dispute turns on the twelve pillars. Wesley leaves it open — the remainder was sprinkled either on the people themselves or on the pillars that represented them. Ellicott closes the option: the words scarcely admit it, and the writer to the Hebrews plainly understood that the people were sprinkled; he allows only that it fell on their representatives, the elders and those standing nearest. Keil takes the consecration as the qualification for what follows: it fitted the Israelites to ascend the mountain and eat the covenant meal — not the whole nation, which was impracticable, but the nation in its representatives, Aaron's two eldest sons being summoned with reference to their future election to the priesthood.

Wesley supplies the theology of the two sprinklings, the fullest thing in the span. The blood put on the altar was the blood of what the people offered, and signified their dedicating themselves to God, all Israel being presented as living sacrifices. The blood put on the people was of a sacrifice God had owned and accepted, and signified his conferring his favour and all its fruits. The words spoken over it seal both ways: see how God seals to you to be a God and you seal to be to him a people, his promises and yours being yea and amen. He carries it forward: the Mediator of the new covenant, of whom Moses was a type, having offered himself on the cross so that his blood might be the blood of the covenant, sprinkled it on the altar in his intercession and sprinkles it on his church by word and ordinances. Clarke reaches the same place in a sentence: the blood of the new covenant was needed to propitiate the throne of justice on one hand and reconcile men to God on the other.
9:
Ellicott explains why the chapter does not end at the sprinkling. By the ideas of the time the ratification was complete; but a sacrifice implied a sacrificial meal, which Moses understood the summons of the first verse to mean was to be held on the mountain. Such a meal was an act done before God, involving communion with him, and God signalised this one by making his presence not merely felt but seen — not amid thunders and darkness but in his loveliness, standing on pellucid sapphire. They saw him and were neither hurt nor terrified, and could still eat and drink like guests at his board. Keil supplies what the narrative leaves unsaid, that when the meal was over the representatives went back down with Moses.

Whether they saw a form divides the span. Henry says they had some glimpse of his glory in light and fire but saw no manner of similitude, his being one whom no man hath seen nor can see; the Greek has them see the place where the God of Israel stood, which came near a similitude and was not. Wesley reproduces this almost word for word. Gill and Ellicott go the other way. Gill insists the sight was corporeal and not a vision of prophecy, and that they saw the Son of God in human form, a presage of his incarnation, rejecting the Targum's hint that their looking was criminal. Ellicott makes the appearance probably human in form, as the prophets saw him, and denies that the later declaration about seeing no similitude refers to this occasion — what they saw had feet.

Of what lay under those feet, three accounts. Henry observes that nothing is described but the pavement, since our conceptions of God are all below him; they saw not so much as his feet, only a splendid work as of sapphires, the heavens being the pavement of God's palace. He turns it into a comparison none of the others make: wisdom was from eternity God's delight and lay in his bosom, while sapphires are only the pavement under his feet — there let us put the wealth of this world, and not in our hearts. Clarke takes the pavement mineralogically, as inlaid work of the kind the Romans left in Britain, argues that sapphire need not be blue so it may have been of many colours, and adds that the Israelites below probably saw it overhead. Ellicott settles the stone as lapis lazuli.

Why the elders survived is answered four times, and three reject the same wrong answer: Gill, Clarke and Calvin all report the reading by which the withheld hand means a withheld gift of prophecy, and all set it aside for the plain sense that God did not strike them. Calvin is most emphatic: the words are violently distorted by that exposition, and the clauses belong together — although they saw God, his hand was not laid on them, but they ate and drank. He grounds the wonder in the ancient proverb that no man shall see God's face and live. The reason it went otherwise, he says, is that they had not rashly thrust themselves forward but come at God's call: our boldness never exceeds its bounds nor can be charged with presumption when founded on God's command, while worse than self-confidence is the timidity that under pretence of modesty distrusts his word. Wesley adds that the splendour was moderated and they strengthened to bear it, so they kept not only their lives but their vigour and comfort — it is of the Lord's mercies we are not consumed. Ellicott ends where Wesley does but names the sacrament: the two facts are concurrent — they both saw God and did eat and drink — and it is impossible, he says, to doubt this forecasts the presence of God realised in the Holy Communion.
12:
The two words be there are read as a warning of length. Henry turns them into a rule — those who would have communion with God must not only come to ordinances but abide by them, blessed being they that dwell in his house and not they that merely call there — adding that Moses taught nothing but what he had received. Ellicott reconstructs the interval: after the meal the company went down into the plain before a second summons came, for Moses and his minister only.

What was promised him divides two of them. Ellicott notices that neither here nor later are the tables expressly said to contain the ten commandments, though it is stated plainly elsewhere — which precludes the fiction of a double decalogue. Calvin denies that the law and commandment promised are any new instruction: the phrase stands in apposition to the tables and explains them, so what was given was the authentic writing of the Law already delivered, written not with ink nor by the hand of man but by the secret power of the Spirit. He then declines an interpretation from a quarter he usually defers to, fearing that Augustine's speculation on the writing by the finger of God is more subtle than correct.

Joshua draws the most varied comment. Ellicott dates his standing from this verse: his command against Amalek showed no more than military capacity, but from here he is plainly the most trusted assistant, and so the successor. Henry adds the reason — he was honoured before the people so they might afterwards take him more readily for their governor; then, following Bishop Pearson, he makes him a type of Christ, since without Jesus, in whom are hid all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge, there is no looking into the secrets of heaven. Wesley gives it in short. Gill asks what none of the others think to ask. Joshua must have been on the mountain the whole forty days, since he knew nothing of the golden calf; did he then fast all that while? There is no necessity to suppose it: the manna fell round about the mountain and he might gather and eat day by day. Clarke and Keil disagree how far up he went: Clarke has Moses leave him in the cloud and ascend to the glory alone, with frequent conferences during the forty days; Keil says we are not told whether he followed, only that a later chapter shows he was on the mountain.

Whether the elders stayed put is a flat two-against-two. Keil reports the order plainly: they were to remain where they were until the return, Aaron and Hur being appointed to judge any matters of dispute. Ellicott makes it stricter — here means the plain below, and the camp was not to move however long the colloquy lasted. Calvin will not take the words so precisely, the adverb indicating our earthly dwelling-place rather than one spot, and the elders being plainly sent back to occupy their charge, which they could not do unless in communication with the people. Clarke agrees they went back, and draws a consequence the others do not: they waited a considerable time and then returned to the camp — their return being supposed the grand cause of the golden calf, since they probably reported that Moses was lost.

On the two regents there is no dispute. Ellicott makes Hur the father of Bezaleel; Henry calls them lords-justices, and notes that Moses would not leave the people as sheep having no shepherd — good princes finding their government a constant care and their people a constant blessing. Calvin doubts whether Moses knew how long he would be gone, and ends on the six days of fire, conspicuous to all from the least to the greatest, so that none could afterwards pretend not to know from what Author the Law proceeded.
15:
Ellicott points out that the article matters — it is the cloud, the one that had accompanied them since they left Succoth. Wesley reads the covering as a lesson: a visible token of God's special presence, since he so shows himself as at the same time to conceal himself, letting us know enough to assure us of his power and grace while intimating that we cannot find him out to perfection. Ellicott gives the waiting a purpose: Moses would not enter without a positive summons, and it pleased God to put it off six days, which he doubtless spent in the prayer and meditation that fitted him for near contact with Deity. Clarke and Wesley both reckon the calendar and reach the same day: the ascent on the first day of the week, so the seventh, on which God spoke, was the sabbath.

Whether the six days belong to the forty gets three answers. Keil says the forty include the six days of waiting, the whole passing without eating or drinking; and he thinks the number significant, since it recurs at the second stay, in Elijah's journey to Horeb, and in the fasting of Jesus. Gill thinks it probable they are counted in, since the text does not say he was in the cloud forty days. Wesley denies it, and his reason is the best here. During those six days Joshua was with Moses and ate of the manna; while they were together it is likely Moses ate with him; but when Moses was called into the midst of the cloud he left Joshua outside, who went on eating daily while he waited — and from that point, not before, Moses fasted.

The fire on the summit is described carefully. Gill insists it was not devouring fire but only like it: so large a body of light that it looked like flames consuming all in their way, and being on the top it was visible throughout the camp. Ellicott says the same from below: to the Israelites in the plain a light like a conflagration rested on the summit the whole time. Clarke draws the apostle's moral, that the appearance was calculated to inspire the deepest reverence and godly fear, our God being a consuming fire. He then offers a second explanation of the golden calf, distinct from the one he gave a few verses earlier: seeing that fire, and Moses having tarried so long, the people probably supposed he had been devoured by it and so fell the more easily into idolatry.

On the entry into the cloud, Gill and Wesley agree what it cost. Gill says Moses must have had more than ordinary courage, the glory flashing out like flames, yet being called he was not intimidated but went in with composure; Wesley calls it an extraordinary presence of mind furnished by grace, without which he durst not have ventured. Gill adds that he entered the cloud after ascending the summit, not before, which the English wording might obscure.

The fast draws one physiological explanation and one sharp aside. Clarke holds that body and soul were so sustained by the invigorating presence of God that Moses needed no earthly support, which may be the simple reason why he took none. Ellicott records the parallels and closes the door: modern imitations of such a fast are in all probability impostures. Clarke ends the chapter with a threefold reflection: that Moses alone was permitted to draw nigh, and was therein a type of Christ, who alone has access to God for the human race; that the law can inspire nothing but terror apart from its sacrifices, and those nothing except as they refer to the Lamb of God; and that the blood sprinkled on altar and people together showed that the death of Christ gave Divine justice what it demanded and men what they needed.
